source_refs.note: Exercise 11.3, Question 6: book page 295. The book prints no answers for Unit 11.

blocks.prompt: 6 (a) A cannonball is fired from the ground at an angle \(30^{\circ}\) with an initial velocity of 100 m/s. Assuming gravity acts downward (\(g = 9.8\) m/s\(^{2}\)) and neglecting air resistance. Formulate the position vector \(\mathbf{r}(t)\) of the cannonball as a function of time.
blocks.explanation:
We must build the position vector of a projectile, as in Example 1 of 11.1.3.
Given: speed 100 m/s at \(30^{\circ}\), \(g = 9.8\) m/s\(^{2}\). Find: \(\mathbf{r}(t)\).
Plan: horizontal motion at constant speed, vertical motion slowed by gravity; put the two components together.
steps:
Given: \(v_{0} = 100\) m/s, \(\theta = 30^{\circ}\), \(g = 9.8\) m/s\(^{2}\).
To find: \(\mathbf{r}(t)\).
Method: take the firing point as the origin, \(\hat{i}\) horizontal and \(\hat{j}\) vertically upward. The projectile model of 11.1.3 (Example 1) is
\[\mathbf{r}(t) = (v_{0}\cos\theta)\,t\,\hat{i}\]
\[\quad + \left((v_{0}\sin\theta)\,t - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^{2}\right)\hat{j}\]

Components of the initial velocity
\[v_{0}\cos 30^{\circ} = 100 \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 50\sqrt{3}\]
\[v_{0}\sin 30^{\circ} = 100 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 50\]
\[\tfrac{1}{2}g = \tfrac{1}{2}(9.8) = 4.9\]
Why: the horizontal part of the velocity is \(v_{0}\cos\theta\) and the vertical part is \(v_{0}\sin\theta\); gravity adds \(-\frac{1}{2}gt^{2}\) to the height.

Position vector
\[\mathbf{r}(t) = 50\sqrt{3}\,t\,\hat{i}\]
\[\quad + (50t - 4.9t^{2})\hat{j}\]
Numerically \(50\sqrt{3} \approx 86.60\), so \(\mathbf{r}(t) \approx 86.60\,t\,\hat{i} + (50t - 4.9t^{2})\hat{j}\) (metres).
Why: substitute the three values into the model.

Check
At \(t = 0\): \(\mathbf{r}(0) = \mathbf{0}\), the firing point. \(\mathbf{r}'(0) = 50\sqrt{3}\,\hat{i} + 50\,\hat{j}\), whose length is \(\sqrt{7500 + 2500} = 100\) m/s at \(\tan^{-1}\frac{50}{50\sqrt{3}} = 30^{\circ}\), as given.

blocks.prompt: 6 (b) A cannonball is fired from the ground at an angle \(30^{\circ}\) with an initial velocity of 100 m/s. Assuming gravity acts downward (\(g = 9.8\) m/s\(^{2}\)) and neglecting air resistance. Find the velocity vector at \(t = 5\) sec.
blocks.explanation:
Velocity is the derivative of the position vector found in part (a).
Find: \(\mathbf{v}(5)\).
Plan: differentiate \(\mathbf{r}(t)\), then put \(t = 5\).
steps:
Given: \(\mathbf{r}(t) = 50\sqrt{3}\,t\,\hat{i} + (50t - 4.9t^{2})\hat{j}\) from part (a).
To find: \(\mathbf{v}(5)\).
Method: \(\mathbf{v}(t) = \mathbf{r}'(t)\), component by component.

Meaning
\[|\mathbf{v}(5)| = \sqrt{(50\sqrt{3})^{2} + 1^{2}}\]
\[= \sqrt{7501} \approx 86.61 \text{ m/s}\]
The vertical component is small and positive, so the ball is still rising very slowly; it reaches its highest point when \(50 - 9.8t = 0\), i.e. at \(t \approx 5.10\) s.
Why: the horizontal velocity never changes (no air resistance); only the vertical part is reduced by gravity.

blocks.prompt: 6 (c) A cannonball is fired from the ground at an angle \(30^{\circ}\) with an initial velocity of 100 m/s. Assuming gravity acts downward (\(g = 9.8\) m/s\(^{2}\)) and neglecting air resistance. Determine the time of the flight (when the cannonball hits the ground).
blocks.explanation:
The ball is on the ground when its height (the \(\hat{j}\)-component) is zero.
Find: the non-zero time when this happens.
Plan: solve \(50t - 4.9t^{2} = 0\) by factorising.
steps:
Given: height \(y(t) = 50t - 4.9t^{2}\) from part (a).
To find: the time of flight \(T\).
Method: the ball lands when \(y(t) = 0\) again.

Set the height to zero
\[50t - 4.9t^{2} = 0\]
\[t(50 - 4.9t) = 0\]
\[t = 0 \ \text{ or } \ t = \dfrac{50}{4.9} = \dfrac{500}{49}\]
Why: a product is zero when a factor is zero. \(t = 0\) is the moment of firing, so the landing time is the other root.

Check
\[T = \dfrac{2v_{0}\sin\theta}{g} = \dfrac{2(100)(0.5)}{9.8}\]
\[= \dfrac{100}{9.8} \approx 10.20 \text{ s}\]
The standard time-of-flight formula agrees. (The ball lands about \(50\sqrt{3} \times \frac{500}{49} \approx 883.70\) m away.)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: The textbook prints no answers for Exercise 11.3 (it prints no answers for any exercise of Unit 11). Every answer on this page is ours: worked out step by step, checked independently with a computer algebra system (sympy) and compared with a solution book. Angles such as \(t = \frac{\pi}{2}\) are in radians.
